title: The Stages of the Wilderness Road
summary: At God's command Moses records every stage of Israel's travel from Rameses in Egypt to the plains of Moab: more than forty camps, from the night after the Passover to the bank of the Jordan, including the death of Aaron on Mount Hor. God then commands Israel, once across the Jordan, to drive out the inhabitants, destroy their idols and high places, and divide the land by lot, warning that those left behind will become thorns in their sides.
story: Numbers is nearly finished, and before Israel crosses the Jordan the book pauses to look back over the whole road. The list reaches back before Numbers itself, through Exodus, to the night Israel left Egypt, and it runs forward to the camp where the people now stand. It is a summary of forty years in a single chapter. Then the chapter turns forward again (verses 50-56), to the task that lies ahead in Canaan. The remaining chapters of the book (34 to 36) deal with the land's borders, its Levitical cities and cities of refuge, and the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters, all in preparation for the conquest that the book of Joshua will narrate.
historical:
Verse 2 says Moses wrote down the stages at the LORD's command, one of the few places in the Pentateuch where Moses is explicitly said to write. Some of the stations are well known from earlier chapters: Rameses and Succoth in the eastern Nile Delta, Marah and Elim, the Desert of Sin, Rephidim, Sinai, Kibroth-hattaavah and Hazeroth (Numbers 11 and 12), Kadesh, and Mount Hor. But many names in the middle of the list (verses 18-35, from Rithmah to Ezion-geber) appear nowhere else in the Bible, and most cannot be located today. Ezion-geber lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba; Kadesh, or Kadesh-barnea, is often identified with the oasis of Ain el-Qudeirat in the northeastern Sinai; and Punon is generally identified with Feinan, an ancient copper-mining area in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea. The location of Mount Sinai itself is debated: the traditional site, Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, goes back to early Christian times, while other scholars propose sites in the northern Sinai or in northwest Arabia.

Verse 38 gives one of the few precise dates in the book: Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after the exodus, at the age of 123.
cultural:
Itineraries of this kind were a known form in the ancient Near East. Assyrian royal inscriptions record military campaigns stage by stage, with the formula departed from one place and camped at another, and Egyptian texts list stations along routes. Israel's list uses the same kind of formula, they set out from and camped at, repeated for each stage. Such lists served as records of real routes and also as memorials, and for Israel each name could call up a story: the bitter water at Marah, the twelve springs at Elim, the thirst at Rephidim, the graves of craving at Kibroth-hattaavah.

The commands of verses 50-56 name three features of Canaanite religion. Carved images and cast idols were figures of gods, set up in shrines and homes. High places were local hilltop sanctuaries, often with altars and standing stones. Israel was to destroy these because they would draw the people into the worship of other gods, as Peor had already shown. The warning that remaining inhabitants would become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” proved true in the book of Judges (Judges 2:1-3).
literary: The chapter is built from a repeated formula, they set out from and camped at, which gives the list a steady marching rhythm. The rhythm is broken at a few points by brief notes that recall major events: the Egyptians burying their firstborn as Israel marched out (verses 3-4), the crossing of the sea (verse 8), the springs and palms of Elim (verse 9), the lack of water at Rephidim (verse 14), and above all the death of Aaron (verses 38-39), the longest note in the list. Many of the great events of the wilderness (the golden calf, the spies, Korah) are passed over without comment. The list is about God's leading, not Israel's failures. After the itinerary, the chapter shifts to divine speech (verses 50-56), turning the record of the past into a charge for the future.

outline.t: Moses records the stages; Israel leaves Egypt
From Rameses to the Wilderness of Sinai
Mount Hor and the death of Aaron
From Mount Hor to the plains of Moab
Drive out the inhabitants and divide the land

doctrines.note: Every stage of the road was recorded because every stage was under God's care. The list is a testimony that God led his people step by step for forty years, through both obedience and rebellion.
God commands Israel to destroy the images and high places of Canaan. Idolatry is treated not as a private matter of taste but as a danger that would destroy the people's covenant with God.
The final warning cuts both ways: if Israel tolerates what God has condemned, he will do to Israel what he planned to do to the Canaanites. God's judgment is not partial toward his own people.

words.note: Massa, a setting out or stage of travel. The word comes from a verb meaning to pull up tent pegs, and so pictures a camp being struck and moved. The chapter's first verse calls the whole list the settings out of the Israelites. Each stage began when the cloud lifted from the tabernacle (9:17-23).

Yarash, to take possession or dispossess. The verb can mean both to inherit or occupy land and to drive out its current occupants. Here it carries both senses: Israel is to drive out the inhabitants and take possession of the land. It becomes one of the key verbs of Deuteronomy and Joshua.

Bamah, high place. The word can mean a height or ridge, but in religious contexts it names a local sanctuary, usually on elevated ground, with an altar. High places are a recurring problem in the books of Kings, where even good kings are faulted for failing to remove them.

christ: Paul reads the wilderness stages as a story written for the church: “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). He even says that the rock from which Israel drank “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), meaning that the God who sustained Israel in the wilderness is the same Lord now known in Jesus. Hebrews describes Abraham and the patriarchs as strangers and exiles on the earth who “were longing for a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). The Christian life is often pictured in the New Testament as a pilgrimage from rescue to promised rest, and this chapter's record of every stage between the Passover and the Jordan gives that picture its Old Testament shape. The connection is one of pattern, drawn by the New Testament writers themselves.

hard.q: Why do the details of this list sometimes differ from other accounts of the wilderness route?
hard.a: Readers who compare this chapter with Exodus, the rest of Numbers, and Deuteronomy notice differences. Some stations here are not mentioned elsewhere, and some places mentioned elsewhere do not appear here. Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah, while this chapter places his death at Mount Hor, several stages after Moseroth. Scholars explain these in different ways. Some suggest that Moserah was a district that included Mount Hor, or that the lists record different kinds of stops. Others think the chapter combines several older route lists, compiled at different times. Still others think the list is selective and arranged for its own purposes, and some have noted that it may be patterned to give a round number of stages. Because many sites cannot be identified, no reconstruction of the whole route has won agreement. What the chapter clearly claims is that Israel's road from Egypt to Moab was real, remembered, and led by God.

questions: The list records every stage but passes over most of Israel's failures in silence. What might it mean to look back on your own life as a record of God's leading?
Many of these places are forgotten today, yet each one was a stop on the road. Which ordinary stages of your life have mattered more than you realized at the time?
God warned that what Israel tolerated would become thorns in their sides. What small compromises are easiest for you to tolerate, and where might they lead?
